value: A calendar-year partnership finishes winding up on 10 August 2025. When is its short-period Form 1065 due, before any weekend adjustment?
reason: 15 November 2025 is a Saturday, so the return is actually timely on Monday 17 November 2025; the front must say it asks for the unadjusted date.

value: The return is due the 15th day of the 3rd month after termination: September, October, November. As 15 November 2025 is a Saturday, filing on Monday 17 November is timely.
reason: Adds the weekend point.

value: A corporation files its 2025 Form 1120 (due in 2026) 70 days late, owing $300 of tax, with no reasonable cause. What late-filing penalty applies?
reason: “due in 2026 70 days late” reads twice; the question is the penalty, which the minimum sets here.

value: 5% × 3 months (a part month counts) × $300 = $45. But a return due in 2026 and over 60 days late has a minimum of the smaller of the tax due or $525: $300.
reason: Works both steps, so it is clear why the minimum, not $45, applies.

value: A corporation owns 30% of another domestic corporation and receives $100,000 of dividends from it (no debt-financing). Its taxable income before the DRD is $500,000. What is its DRD?
reason: Without taxable income, the section 246(b) taxable income limit could cut the deduction below $65,000.

value: 30% ownership is 20% or more, so 65% applies: $100,000 × 65% = $65,000. The taxable income limit does not bite: 65% × $500,000 is far above that.
reason: Shows why the section 246(b) limit (i1120 p. 19, “Line 9, Column (c)”) does not reduce it.

value: The third exception is stock received for the corporation’s debt (other than a security), or for interest on its debt that accrued while you held it.
reason: “Ordinary debt” is not the source’s term: Publication 542 p. 3 says “debt (other than a security) or for interest on the corporation's debt (including a security) that accrued while you held the debt”.

value: But nonshareholder contributions made after 22 December 2017 by a civic group, a governmental entity or a customer (in aid of construction) are not nontaxable paid-in capital.
reason: “Since … excluded from this” reads twice; Publication 542 p. 4 says “after December 22, 2017, the following nonshareholder contributions … are not considered nontaxable paid-in capital”.

value: Not a personal service corporation; five or fewer individuals own over 50% of its stock value at any time in the year’s last half.
reason: “During the year’s last half” suggests the whole half; the source says “At any time during the last half of the tax year”.

value: Outside that window, relief is still possible if the corporation and all shareholders reported as an S corporation, 6 months have passed since its first return, and no IRS notice followed.
reason: The old text gave one of three conditions as if it were enough. i2553 p. 2 item 6: consistent reporting, “At least 6 months have elapsed…”, and no IRS notice “within 6 months”.

value: An S corporation starts 2025 with AAA of $30,000. For 2025 it has ordinary income of $50,000, tax-exempt interest of $2,000, nondeductible expenses of $1,000 (none tied to tax-exempt income) and cash distributions of $60,000. Year-end AAA?
reason: Nondeductible expenses related to tax-exempt income do not reduce AAA (i1120s p. 50), so the front must say these are not.

value: A calendar-year corporation wants S status from 1 January 2025. What is the latest it can file Form 2553 during 2025 without needing late-election relief?
reason: Late-election relief (i2553 p. 2) allows a Form 2553 up to 3 years and 75 days late, so “latest” needs this limit.
